form: compound — *full* + *fledged*, from a bird with all its feathers grown
contrast: American *full-fledged*; British writing says *fully fledged*.

senses.gloss: Completely developed, or having reached full status.
examples: She's now a *full-fledged* attorney.
What started as a hobby became a *full-fledged* business.
The protest grew into a *full-fledged* movement.

senses.gloss: Having reached full adult size.
examples: A *full-grown* male can weigh 600 pounds.
The tree isn't *full-grown* yet.
She has three *full-grown* children.

ru: полнометражный; в полный рост, до пола

senses.gloss: Of a movie, album or book: of the normal, complete length.
examples: Their first *full-length* album comes out in May.
It's a *full-length* documentary, not a short.

senses.gloss: Reaching the whole height or length of something.
examples: There's a *full-length* mirror in the bedroom.
She wore a *full-length* gown.

contrast: Informal. It is also an adverb meaning 'completely': *She went full on into training*.

senses.gloss: Complete and not held back in any way.
examples: It wasn't a disagreement — it was a *full-on* argument.
They're in *full-on* panic mode.
He greeted me with a *full-on* bear hug.

senses.gloss: Filling a whole page.
examples: They took out a *full-page* ad in the Times.
The magazine ran a *full-page* photo of the crash.
Each chapter opens with a *full-page* illustration.

senses.gloss: As large or as complete as it can be.
examples: The country is on the edge of a *full-scale* war.
Police launched a *full-scale* investigation.

senses.gloss: Of a model or drawing: the same size as the real thing.
examples: The museum has a *full-scale* replica of the shuttle.
They built a *full-scale* mock-up of the cockpit.

contrast: Also *full-sized*. Of a bed, *full-size* names a standard American size between a twin and a queen.

senses.gloss: Of the normal, full size rather than a smaller version.
examples: We rented a *full-size* SUV.
The apartment has a *full-size* kitchen.
They sleep in a *full-size* bed.

senses.gloss: Loud and with no holding back, whether a sound or a show of support.
examples: He gave a *full-throated* defense of the policy.
The crowd let out a *full-throated* roar.
The senator offered *full-throated* support for the bill.

contrast: *fun* means you enjoy it; *funny* means it makes you laugh. *a fun movie* is entertaining, *a funny movie* is a comedy. *fun* is also a noun (*We had a lot of fun*), and *funner*/*funnest* are children's forms.

senses.gloss: Enjoyable; giving pleasure.
examples: We had a *fun* weekend at the lake.
She's a *fun* person to work with.
Skiing turned out to be *more fun* than I expected.

senses.gloss: Full of enjoyable activities.
examples: The resort promises a *fun-filled* weekend.
They spent a *fun-filled* afternoon at the fair.
It was three *fun-filled* days of music and food.

senses.gloss: Enjoying parties, jokes and good times.
examples: He's a *fun-loving* guy who never takes things too seriously.
They're a *fun-loving* family.
Her *fun-loving* side comes out on vacation.

contrast: A *dysfunctional* family is not one that fails to work in this sense — *dysfunctional* means unhealthy relationships.

senses.gloss: Working, and able to be used.
examples: Only one of the elevators is *functional*.
The kitchen is small but fully *functional*.

senses.gloss: Designed to be practical rather than attractive.
examples: The furniture is plain and *functional*.
It's a *functional* building, not a beautiful one.
The new layout is *more functional* than the old one.

senses.gloss: Relating to the way something works.
examples: There's no *functional* difference between the two models.
The scan showed no *functional* damage.

contrast: In *The machine is functioning* this is the verb, not the adjective.

senses.gloss: Working as it should.
examples: It's the only *functioning* hospital in the region.
They want a *functioning* government, not a caretaker.
A fully *functioning* immune system clears the virus in days.

contrast: The noun *the fundamentals* means the basics: *the fundamentals of accounting*.

senses.gloss: Forming the base of something, and therefore the most important.
examples: There's a *fundamental* difference between the two plans.
Free speech is *fundamental* to a democracy.
The problem is *more fundamental* than a software bug.

contrast: Also a noun: *He was raised by fundamentalists*.

senses.gloss: Following the strictest, most literal form of a religion or belief.
examples: He was raised in a *fundamentalist* church.
The party has taken a *fundamentalist* line.
Her reading of the text is strictly *fundamentalist*.

senses.gloss: Paid for with money provided for the purpose.
examples: The program is *funded* by the state.
She works in a well-*funded* research lab.
Is the project fully *funded* yet?

senses.gloss: Caused by or consisting of fungus.
examples: She's being treated for a *fungal* infection.
*Fungal* growth ruined the crop.
It's a *fungal* disease that spreads in wet weather.

contrast: A law and finance word, familiar to most people from *non-fungible token*.

senses.gloss: Able to be exchanged for another unit of exactly the same kind.
examples: Money is *fungible* — one dollar is as good as another.
These parts are *fungible*, so any supplier will do.
*Fungible* goods can be replaced one for one.

senses.gloss: Unusual and stylish in a relaxed, offbeat way.
examples: She wears *funky* glasses.
It's a *funky* little coffee shop on Third.
The place got *funkier* after the new owners took over.

senses.gloss: Of music: with a strong, danceable rhythm.
examples: The band has a *funky* bass line.
I love the *funky* stuff they recorded in the seventies.

senses.gloss: Smelling bad.
examples: Something in the fridge smells *funky*.
His gym bag is seriously *funky*.

senses.gloss: Having fur on the inside for warmth.
examples: She pulled on her *fur-lined* boots.
He wore a parka with a *fur-lined* hood.
The gloves are *fur-lined*.

contrast: *furnished* means it has furniture. The furniture itself is *the furnishings*.

senses.gloss: Supplied with furniture.
examples: We're renting a *furnished* apartment near campus.
The place comes fully *furnished*.
Is the room *furnished*, or do we bring a bed?

senses.gloss: Covered with fur, or soft like fur.
examples: A *furry* little dog ran up to us.
The blanket is soft and *furry*.
Her cat gets *furrier* every winter.

senses.gloss: Done quietly and secretly, so that nobody notices.
examples: He took a *furtive* glance at his phone.
They exchanged *furtive* looks across the table.
There was something *furtive* about the way she left.

contrast: *picky* is the everyday American word for the first sense: *a picky eater*.

senses.gloss: Hard to please, and worried about small details.
examples: He's *fussy* about what he eats.
Don't be so *fussy* — it's just a sandwich.
She's *fussier* than her sister about grammar.

senses.gloss: Of a baby: crying and unsettled.
examples: The baby's *fussy* tonight.
He gets *fussy* around bedtime.

senses.gloss: Of a design: crowded with too many small details.
examples: The wallpaper is a little *fussy* for my taste.
The dress is pretty, but the lace is *fussy*.

senses.gloss: Certain to fail, so not worth doing.
examples: It was a *futile* attempt to save the building.
Arguing with him is *futile*.
Every effort so far has proved *futile*.

senses.gloss: Looking as if it belongs to the future.
examples: The car has a *futuristic* dashboard.
The building looks *futuristic* against the old skyline.
Their designs are *more futuristic* than practical.

contrast: *warm and fuzzy* is a fixed phrase for a comfortable, sentimental feeling: *The ad gave me a warm and fuzzy feeling*.

senses.gloss: Covered with short soft hairs.
examples: He gave her a *fuzzy* teddy bear.
The peaches were warm and *fuzzy*.

senses.gloss: Not clear or sharp, whether a picture, a memory or a rule.
examples: The photo came out *fuzzy*.
My memory of that night is *fuzzy*.
The rules get *fuzzier* the more you read them.

contrast: Almost only in *gainful employment* and the adverb *gainfully employed*.

senses.gloss: Paid; providing an income.
examples: He's looking for *gainful* employment.
The visa requires *gainful* work.
She hasn't held a *gainful* job in years.

contrast: A false friend to watch: Russian *галантный* covers only the second sense. The first sense — brave — is the commoner one in English, and often describes a brave loss.

senses.gloss: Brave, especially in a fight that is being lost.
examples: They put up a *gallant* fight.
It was a *gallant* effort, but they lost by two.
No army was *more gallant* in defeat.

senses.gloss: Of a man: polite and attentive toward women.
examples: He was *gallant* enough to carry her bags.
A *gallant* older gentleman held the door.

comparison: not gradable — but the 'stirred to action' sense takes *more/most*

senses.gloss: Of metal: covered with zinc so that it will not rust.
examples: The roof is *galvanized* steel.
Use *galvanized* nails outdoors.

senses.gloss: Shocked into sudden action.
examples: The town was *galvanized* by the news.
Voters seem *galvanized* this year.

contrast: Don't confuse the adjective with the noun *game*. *a game player* is read as somebody who plays games, so put the adjective after a verb: *He's game*.

senses.gloss: Willing to try something, especially something new or risky.
examples: I'm *game* if you are.
She's always *game* for a road trip.
He was *game* to try anything once.

form: compound — noun + *-changing*, from the phrase *change the game*

senses.gloss: So important that it changes how everything is done.
examples: The drug has been *game-changing* for these patients.
They call it a *game-changing* technology.
Cheap storage was a *game-changing* development.

contrast: Also *gangling*, with the same meaning.

senses.gloss: Tall and thin, and awkward in the way of a growing teenager.
examples: A *gangly* teenager answered the door.
He was tall and *gangly* at sixteen.
The colt looked *ganglier* than the rest.

senses.gloss: Of a hole or a wound: wide open.
examples: There was a *gaping* hole in the roof.
The crash left a *gaping* wound in his side.
That leaves a *gaping* hole in their defense.

senses.gloss: So confused or distorted that it is hard to understand.
examples: The message came through *garbled*.
He gave a *garbled* account of what happened.
The recording is *more garbled* than the first one.

contrast: American; British English says *common-or-garden*.

senses.gloss: Ordinary; of the most common kind.
examples: It's just a *garden-variety* cold.
This is a *garden-variety* contract dispute.
He's a *garden-variety* con man, nothing more.

senses.gloss: Enormous.
examples: They served a *gargantuan* plate of ribs.
The project is a *gargantuan* undertaking.
His appetite is *gargantuan*.

senses.gloss: Too bright or too colorful, in a way that looks cheap.
examples: The lobby is painted a *garish* orange.
She thought the decorations were *garish*.
The signs get *more garish* every year.

senses.gloss: Talking too much, especially about small things.
examples: Our *garrulous* neighbor kept us on the porch for an hour.
He gets *garrulous* after two drinks.
She's the *most garrulous* person in the office.

contrast: American *gas* is gasoline (British *petrol*), so a *gas-powered* car runs on gasoline, not on natural gas.

senses.gloss: Running on gasoline.
examples: They still drive a *gas-powered* car.
The mower is *gas-powered*.
*Gas-powered* leaf blowers are banned in the city.

senses.gloss: In the form of a gas.
examples: Water can be solid, liquid or *gaseous*.
The *gaseous* state takes up far more room.
They studied the planet's *gaseous* outer layer.

senses.gloss: Having uncomfortable gas in the stomach.
examples: Beans make me *gassy*.
The baby's *gassy* and won't go down.

senses.gloss: Of a drink: with too many bubbles.
examples: This beer is *gassier* than I like.
He won't touch *gassy* soda.

senses.gloss: Relating to the stomach.
examples: She had *gastric* bypass surgery.
*Gastric* acid breaks the food down.
He's being treated for a *gastric* ulcer.

contrast: Usually shortened to *GI* in speech and charts: *a GI infection*.

senses.gloss: Relating to the stomach and the intestines.
examples: The drug can cause *gastrointestinal* problems.
He was admitted with *gastrointestinal* bleeding.
It's a common *gastrointestinal* virus.

senses.gloss: Closed off by a gate, so that only certain people can get in.
examples: They bought a house in a *gated* community.
The parking lot is *gated* after nine.
A *gated* driveway leads up to the house.

contrast: *gaudy*, *garish* and *flashy* all criticize. *flashy* can be half-admiring; *gaudy* almost never is.

senses.gloss: Too bright and showy to be in good taste.
examples: He wore a *gaudy* gold watch.
The costumes were *gaudy* and cheap-looking.
Her jewelry gets *gaudier* every year.

senses.gloss: Very thin and bony, usually from illness, hunger or worry.
examples: He came back from the hospital *gaunt* and pale.
Her *gaunt* face shocked all of us.
The prisoners looked even *more gaunt* than in the photographs.

senses.gloss: Thin and light enough to see through.
examples: *Gauzy* curtains filtered the afternoon light.
She wore a *gauzy* summer dress.
The fabric is *gauzier* than it looked online.

senses.gloss: Awkward in the way you move, especially because you are young and tall.
examples: He was a *gawky* kid with big glasses.
She felt *gawky* at the school dance.
Teenagers usually look *gawkier* than they feel.

contrast: In books written before about 1960, *gay* means 'cheerful, bright'. That sense is now only historical, and using it today would be misread.

senses.gloss: Sexually attracted to people of one's own sex; relating to gay people.
examples: They're a *gay* couple from Chicago.
He came out as *gay* in college.
The city has a large *gay* community.

senses.gloss: Thick, wobbly and sticky, like jelly.
examples: The sauce cooled into a *gelatinous* blob.
Jellyfish are soft and *gelatinous*.
The pudding came out *more gelatinous* than it should be.

senses.gloss: Not marked as male or female; usable by anyone.
examples: The restroom on this floor is *gender-neutral*.
They picked a *gender-neutral* name for the baby.
The form uses *gender-neutral* language throughout.

senses.gloss: Treating men and women differently, or marked for grammatical gender.
examples: *Gendered* language is common in the older textbooks.
Toy aisles are still heavily *gendered*.
Spanish nouns are *gendered*; English nouns are not.

senses.gloss: Relating to family history and descent.
examples: She does *genealogical* research on weekends.
The library keeps *genealogical* records going back to 1820.
He traced the family through a *genealogical* database.

ru: общий, всеобщий; в общих чертах; главный
contrast: Also a noun — an army rank (*General Lee*). The phrase *in general* and the adverb *generally* carry the first sense.

senses.gloss: Affecting most people or things, and not limited to a few.
examples: There's a *general* feeling that things are improving.
The *general* public was never told.
The strike caused *general* disruption downtown.

senses.gloss: Broad rather than detailed.
examples: Give me the *general* idea first.
Her answer was too *general* to be useful.
Let's start with something *more general* and narrow it down.

senses.gloss: Highest in rank, or covering all areas of a job.
examples: She's the company's *general* counsel.
The *general* manager made the call.

contrast: American spelling with *-ized*; British writing has *generalised*.

senses.gloss: Made to apply widely instead of to one case, often too widely.
examples: That's a *generalized* statement with no evidence behind it.
The findings are too *generalized* to help us.

senses.gloss: In medicine: affecting the whole body rather than one spot.
examples: He came in with a *generalized* rash.
She was diagnosed with *generalized* anxiety disorder.

senses.gloss: Relating to the differences between one generation and the next.
examples: There's a *generational* divide over the issue.
The split here is *generational*, not political.

senses.gloss: Passed down through generations, or seen only once in a generation.
senses.ru: передающийся из поколения в поколение; исключительный
examples: He's a *generational* talent at quarterback.
The family built *generational* wealth.

contrast: Most people now meet the word in *generative AI*.

senses.gloss: Able to produce something new.
examples: *Generative* AI writes the first draft.
He studies *generative* grammar.
The tool runs on a *generative* model.

senses.gloss: Of a product: sold without a brand name.
examples: Ask for the *generic* version — it's a third of the price.
The pharmacy filled it with a *generic* drug.

senses.gloss: Not specific; without any character of its own.
examples: His answer was pretty *generic*.
The hotel room was clean but *generic*.
Every reply got *more generic* as the day went on.

contrast: The adverb is *genetically*: *genetically modified corn*.

senses.gloss: Relating to genes, or passed on through them.
examples: The condition is *genetic*.
They ran a *genetic* test on both parents.
There's a *genetic* link between the two diseases.

senses.gloss: Aimed at destroying a whole people.
examples: The report describes a *genocidal* campaign.
He was charged with *genocidal* intent.
Their rhetoric has turned openly *genocidal*.

senses.gloss: Relating to the whole set of genes in an organism.
examples: The lab does *genomic* sequencing.
*Genomic* data helped identify the new strain.
She works in *genomic* medicine.

contrast: Often faintly mocking: it suggests good manners kept up for show, sometimes after the money is gone. Not the same word as *gentle*.

senses.gloss: Polite and refined, in a careful, old-fashioned way.
examples: They live in *genteel* poverty in a big old house.
The tearoom has a *genteel* atmosphere.
Her manners were *genteel* to the point of stiffness.

form: -ly from *gentleman* — an adjective, not an adverb
contrast: An *-ly* adjective with no matching adverb: say *He behaved in a gentlemanly way*, not *He behaved gentlemanly*.

senses.gloss: Behaving with the courtesy expected of a well-mannered man.
examples: That was a very *gentlemanly* thing to do.
He made a *gentlemanly* apology.
His conduct was *gentlemanly* throughout the argument.

senses.gloss: Of a poor neighborhood: changed by richer people moving in, so that prices rise.
examples: The neighborhood is completely *gentrified* now.
She misses the bodegas the *gentrified* blocks lost.
The area gets *more gentrified* every year.

contrast: *genuine* and *authentic* overlap, but a *genuine* person is sincere, while an *authentic* dish is true to where it comes from.

senses.gloss: Real, and not a copy.
examples: Is that a *genuine* Rolex?
The painting turned out to be *genuine* after all.

senses.gloss: Sincere; meaning what you say.
examples: She showed *genuine* concern.
He's a *genuine* guy — what you see is what you get.
Her surprise looked *more genuine* than his.

contrast: *geographic* and *geographical* mean the same thing; *geographic* is a little more common in American English.

senses.gloss: Relating to the physical features or the layout of places.
examples: The map shows the main *geographic* features.
Sales are broken out by *geographic* region.
Families here face *geographic* barriers to care.

senses.gloss: Relating to geography, or to where things are on the map.
examples: The study covers a wide *geographical* area.
There are *geographical* limits to the service.
They looked for *geographical* patterns in the data.

contrast: American technical writing often shortens it to *geologic*: *the geologic record*.

senses.gloss: Relating to the rocks of the earth and how they formed.
examples: The canyon took millions of years of *geological* change.
They ran a *geological* survey of the site.
*Geological* evidence points to an ancient lake.

senses.gloss: Made of regular shapes and straight lines.
examples: The rug has a bold *geometric* pattern.
Her later paintings are strictly *geometric*.

senses.gloss: Relating to geometry; of growth, multiplying rather than adding.
examples: Cases were rising at a *geometric* rate.
It's a *geometric* progression, not an arithmetic one.

senses.gloss: Relating to how geography shapes power between countries.
examples: The war has *geopolitical* consequences far beyond the region.
Oil has always been a *geopolitical* weapon.
They weighed the *geopolitical* risk before investing.

senses.gloss: Using heat from inside the earth.
examples: Iceland runs largely on *geothermal* energy.
They installed a *geothermal* heat pump.
The plant taps *geothermal* steam a mile down.

comparison: not gradable — but the joking sense takes *very*
contrast: Calling a person *geriatric* outside a medical setting is an insult.

senses.gloss: Relating to the medical care of old people.
examples: She's a *geriatric* nurse.
The hospital opened a *geriatric* unit last spring.

senses.gloss: Joking and rude: too old to work well any more.
examples: My *geriatric* laptop takes ten minutes to boot.
At thirty-four he's *geriatric* by gymnastics standards.

senses.gloss: With no germs on or in it.
examples: The lab keeps the mice *germ-free*.
No kitchen is ever completely *germ-free*.
They advertise a *germ-free* surface.

contrast: Formal, and common in law and debate. The everyday word is *relevant*.

senses.gloss: Closely connected to the matter being discussed.
examples: That question isn't *germane* to the discussion.
Only *germane* amendments may be offered.
His past record is *more germane* here than you think.

senses.gloss: Relating to pregnancy and the time the baby is carried.
examples: She developed *gestational* diabetes in month six.
The doctor estimated the *gestational* age.
They worked with a *gestational* carrier.

senses.gloss: Terrible and shocking.
examples: It was a *ghastly* accident.
The weather has been *ghastly* all week.
The food got *ghastlier* as the trip went on.

senses.gloss: Very pale and ill-looking.
examples: He looked *ghastly* after the overnight flight.
She turned a *ghastly* white.

senses.gloss: Taking an unhealthy interest in death and suffering.
examples: He has a *ghoulish* interest in true crime.
The photos the paper ran were *ghoulish*.
There was something *ghoulish* about the way the crowd watched.

contrast: Also a noun (*a giant*). Before a noun it is ordinary English, but after a verb use *huge* or *gigantic*: *The oak is gigantic*, not *The oak is giant*.

senses.gloss: Very large.
examples: A *giant* oak shades the whole yard.
They ordered a *giant* pizza.
The company took a *giant* step forward this year.

senses.gloss: Feeling dizzy, as if everything is turning.
examples: The heat made her *giddy*.
I stood up too fast and felt *giddy*.

senses.gloss: Excited and a little silly with happiness.
examples: The kids were *giddy* on Christmas Eve.
He was *giddy* with relief.
She got *giddier* the closer we came to the gate.

form: -ed from the noun *gift*, in the sense 'natural talent'
contrast: Nothing to do with receiving presents. The *-ed* is a full syllable: GIF-tid.

senses.gloss: Having a great natural ability.
examples: She's a *gifted* pianist.
The district runs a program for *gifted* students.
He's *more gifted* than he lets on.

senses.gloss: Laughing in a nervous or silly way, and unable to stop.
examples: The girls got *giggly* at the back of the bus.
She's *giggly* whenever she's nervous.
The class grew *gigglier* as the hour went on.

senses.gloss: Covered with a thin layer of gold.
examples: A *gilded* frame held the mirror.
The dome is *gilded* and can be seen for miles.

senses.gloss: Rich and protected by wealth.
examples: They grew up in a *gilded* world.
Historians call the 1880s America's *Gilded* Age.

senses.gloss: Relying on a clever trick to attract attention, rather than on real quality.
examples: The new feature feels *gimmicky*.
It's a *gimmicky* restaurant with a surprisingly good kitchen.
Their ads get *more gimmicky* every season.

senses.gloss: Like a girl, or suited to a young girl.
examples: She gave a *girlish* laugh.
His voice is still a little *girlish*.
There was something *girlish* about her round handwriting.

position: both — the 'particular' sense before a noun, the 'tending to' sense after a verb
takes: *to* + noun or *-ing* in the 'tending to' sense
contrast: *given* is also a preposition (*Given the weather, we stayed in*) and a noun (*It's a given that he'll be late*).

senses.gloss: Particular; already fixed or stated.
examples: Only thirty people may be in the room at any *given* time.

senses.gloss: Having a habit of doing something.
examples: He's *given* to long silences.

comparison: not gradable — but the 'slow' and 'cold in manner' senses take *more/most*

senses.gloss: Relating to glaciers or to the ice ages.
examples: The valley was cut by *glacial* ice.

senses.gloss: Extremely slow.
examples: Progress has been *glacial*.
The line moved at a *glacial* pace.

senses.gloss: Very cold and unfriendly.
examples: She gave him a *glacial* stare.
The tone of the email was *glacial*.

senses.gloss: Attractive and exciting in a rich, stylish way.
examples: She looked *glamorous* in a long black dress.
The job sounds *glamorous*, but it's mostly email.
Their parties got *more glamorous* every year.

senses.gloss: Hitting or touching at an angle rather than straight on — also of a brief mention.
examples: The car took a *glancing* blow to the fender.
He made only a *glancing* reference to the scandal.
It was a *glancing* hit, not a direct one.

contrast: British *glandular fever* is American *mono*, short for mononucleosis.

senses.gloss: Relating to the glands of the body.
examples: The doctor suspects a *glandular* problem.
*Glandular* tissue swells during the illness.
It's a *glandular* disorder, not a matter of diet.

senses.gloss: Very obvious, and bad.
examples: There's a *glaring* error on the first page.
The report has *glaring* omissions.
The gap is *more glaring* this year than last.

senses.gloss: Of light: unpleasantly bright.
examples: The *glaring* sun made it hard to see the road.
She squinted in the *glaring* white light of the hallway.

contrast: *a glass door* uses the noun *glass*; *glassy* never means 'made of glass', only 'like glass'.

senses.gloss: Smooth and shiny like glass.
examples: The lake was *glassy* at dawn.
The water got *glassier* as the wind died down.

senses.gloss: Of eyes: fixed and showing no feeling.
examples: He stared at me with *glassy* eyes.
Her eyes went *glassy* with fever.

contrast: For eyes, the usual phrase is *glazed over*: *My eyes glazed over halfway through*.

senses.gloss: Covered with a shiny coating, especially food.
examples: He ate two *glazed* donuts on the way in.
The ham is *glazed* with brown sugar.

senses.gloss: Of eyes: dull and showing no interest.
examples: By the third hour their eyes were *glazed*.
He had a *glazed* look and hadn't heard a word.

senses.gloss: Shining brightly, usually because it is clean or new.
examples: The kitchen was *gleaming* after she scrubbed it.
A *gleaming* new truck sat in the driveway.
His shoes were *gleaming*.

contrast: Often carries a hint of enjoying somebody else's trouble.

senses.gloss: Openly delighted, sometimes at another's expense.
examples: The kids were *gleeful* when school was canceled.
He wore a *gleeful* grin all afternoon.
The commentators were *gleeful* about the upset.

contrast: Always a criticism: smooth talk that comes too easily to be sincere.

senses.gloss: Spoken easily and smoothly, but without real thought or honesty.
examples: He gave a *glib* answer and moved on.
That's a *glib* explanation for a complicated problem.
The more he talked, the *glibber* he sounded.

senses.gloss: Shining faintly and unsteadily.
examples: *Glimmering* lights lined the harbor.
A *glimmering* strip of water showed between the trees.
The candles were still *glimmering* at midnight.

senses.gloss: Giving off small quick flashes of reflected light.
examples: Sunlight caught the *glinting* metal of the roof.
I saw something *glinting* in the grass.
Her *glinting* eyes gave the joke away.

contrast: *glistening* is the shine of something wet; *gleaming* is the shine of something clean or polished.

senses.gloss: Shining because it is wet or oily.
examples: His forehead was *glistening* with sweat.
*Glistening* snow covered the field.
The seals lay on the *glistening* rocks.

senses.gloss: Of software or equipment: full of small faults that make it work badly.
examples: The app is *glitchy* on older phones.
The video feed got *glitchier* as more people joined.
It's a *glitchy* build, but it works well enough to demo.
